Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Her powerful voice resonates through the music hall, delivering an unlikely message of hope. All eight Liyana band members met at the King George VI school for disabled children in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. The Afro-fusion melody comes from an unlikely source -- the small, wheelchair-ridden body of Prudence Mabhena, a woman from Zimbabwe who has overcome her physical disabilities and the hurdles of daily life in her home country. "Some people don't even get you and take you as a person," Mabhena said. "And with us singing right now, we're not giving up -- we're pushing up." Mabhena is the lead singer of Liyana, a group of eight musicians who are all physically disabled and from Zimbabwe. Their message of hope has been drowned out in their home country, which is suffering from an economic collapse, a cholera outbreak, and a political power struggle that has erupted into violence.  Watch the band performing » . Mabhena was born with arthrogryphosis, a muscle and joint disorder, and had to have parts of her arms and legs amputated as a result. She said her mother was told to kill her rather than have her face life as a physically disabled woman in Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe was once a center for disability rights after it gained independence in 1980, according to recent report on Public Radio International. It was one of the first countries to recognize the rights of the disabled, who are sometimes shunned by communities in rural Africa who fear they are touched by witchcraft. But the gains for the disabled in Zimbabwe have been erased by the country's current crisis, according to Dr. Raymond Lang of the London-based Cheshire Center for Conflict Recovery who spoke to PRI's Lonny Shavelson. Mabhena said the group is apprehensive about returning to Zimbabwe after its U.S. tour, which wrapped up this month. But none of the members of Liyana dwell on the despair. "'Never give up' -- it's one of our biggest and strongest mottos," said singer Tapiwa Nyenger, explaining one of the band's song titles. "We have the capability to go on stage and at the end of the day make people smile. It's a good feeling." All eight band members, who are between the ages of 17 and 23, met at the King George VI school for disabled children in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. The band describes their music as a fusion between "myriad geographic, cultural, and musical genres including gospel, reggae, and traditional Zimbabwean Shona music." Liyana means "rain" -- a Shona term for good luck. "Music makes you think of something positive," Nyenger said. "For me, music is rehabilitation." Mabhena has said her voice is a gift from god. They had long dreamed of performing in the United States, and their multi-city tour included more than 20 performances in California and the New York metro area, including the New Jersey Performing Arts Center in Newark. "We have been received in an overwhelming, heart-filling way," Nyenger said. "Everywhere we go, every place we go, we [see] new things, we meet new people, we learn new stuff." The band's U.S. tour coincided with President Barack Obama's inauguration, which has also been a source of inspiration for a new song, "Obama." "When we heard Obama was going to be the American president, the first black American president, we were so excited," Mabhena said. "Through that joy that we had, there came a song." Liyana is also the subject of a new documentary, iTemba -- My Hope -- which is scheduled to be released worldwide later this year. The band's singers perform in seven languages -- Shona, Ndebele, English, Dutch, German, Hebrew, and Spanish -- allowing them to reach a wider audience. "We want to leave a message to everyone in the world that no matter what circumstance you are in, you can make it," singer Marvelous Meulo said.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) -- Her powerful voice resonates through the music hall, delivering an unlikely message of hope. The Afro-fusion melody emanates from an unexpected source—the small, wheelchair-bound frame of Prudence Mabhena, a Zimbabwean woman who has triumphed over both her physical disabilities and the daily hardships of life in her homeland. "Some people don't even understand you—they don't see you as a person," Mabhena said. "But through our singing, we're showing that we're not giving up—we're rising up."

Mabhena is the lead singer of Liyana, an ensemble of eight musicians, all of whom are physically disabled and hail from Zimbabwe. Yet their message of hope has been largely overshadowed in their home country, which continues to grapple with economic collapse, a cholera outbreak, and a political power struggle that has descended into violence.

Watch the band performing »

Mabhena was born with arthrogryposis, a disorder affecting the muscles and joints, which necessitated the amputation of portions of her arms and legs. She has revealed that her mother was once urged to end her life rather than allow her to endure the challenges of living as a disabled woman in Zimbabwe.

According to a recent report by Public Radio International, Zimbabwe was once regarded as a pioneer in disability rights following its independence in 1980, becoming one of the first nations to formally recognize the rights of disabled individuals—a population often marginalized in rural African communities due to superstitious beliefs linking disability to witchcraft. However, these hard-won advances have since been undone by the nation's ongoing crisis, according to Dr. Raymond Lang of the London-based Cheshire Centre for Conflict Recovery, who spoke with PRI's Lonny Shavelson.

Mabhena admits the group harbors apprehension about returning to Zimbabwe following the conclusion of their U.S. tour this month. Yet none of Liyana's members allow themselves to dwell on despair. "'Never give up'—that's one of our strongest mottos," said singer Tapiwa Nyenger, referencing one of the band's song titles. "We have the ability to step on stage and, by the end of the day, bring smiles to people's faces. It's an incredible feeling."

All eight members of the band, ranging in age from 17 to 23, first came together at the King George VI School for disabled children in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. The group describes their sound as a fusion of "myriad geographic, cultural, and musical genres, including gospel, reggae, and traditional Zimbabwean Shona music." The name Liyana, meaning "rain" in Shona, symbolizes good fortune.

"Music inspires you to think positively," Nyenger reflected. "For me, music is a form of rehabilitation." Mabhena, for her part, has described her singing voice as a gift from God.

Having long dreamed of performing in the United States, the band fulfilled that ambition with a multi-city tour comprising more than 20 performances across California and the New York metropolitan area, including a stop at the New Jersey Performing Arts Center in Newark. "We have been welcomed in the most overwhelming and heartwarming way," Nyenger said. "Everywhere we go, we encounter new experiences, meet new people, and continue to learn."

The band's American tour coincided with President Barack Obama's inauguration—an event that inspired their new song, aptly titled "Obama." "When we learned that Obama would become the first Black American president, we were overjoyed," Mabhena recalled. "That joy gave birth to a song."

Liyana is also the subject of an upcoming documentary, iTemba—My Hope, set for worldwide release later this year. The band performs in seven languages—Shona, Ndebele, English, Dutch, German, Hebrew, and Spanish—enabling them to connect with audiences across the globe.

"We want to leave the world with a message: no matter your circumstances, you can overcome them," said singer Marvelous Meulo.

# CNN, Her, and All: A Reflection on Media, Identity, and Connection

In today's interconnected world, the ways we consume information and form our identities have become deeply intertwined with media, technology, and personal narrative. Considering CNN, "Her," and the concept of "All" together offers an interesting lens through which to examine modern life.

## The Information Age: CNN's Role

CNN, as one of the world's most prominent 24-hour news networks, represents our collective hunger for constant information. Since its founding in 1980, CNN has shaped how millions of people understand global events, politics, and culture. The network exemplifies both the power and the challenges of modern journalism—the immediacy of breaking news, the pressure to fill airtime, and the responsibility of shaping public discourse. CNN's presence in our daily lives raises important questions about how constant news consumption affects our mental state, our worldview, and our sense of connection to events happening far beyond our immediate experience.

## Her: Intimacy in the Digital Age

Spike Jonze's 2013 film "Her" offers a poignant counterpoint to the constant noise of media like CNN. The film explores loneliness, connection, and what it means to form relationships in an increasingly digital world. Through the story of a man who falls in love with an AI operating system, "Her" asks profound questions about intimacy, authenticity, and whether meaningful connection can exist without physical presence. As artificial intelligence becomes more sophisticated in our own reality, the film feels increasingly prophetic, challenging us to consider what we truly need from relationships and how technology might both bridge and create emotional distances.

## All: The Search for Wholeness

The word "All" suggests completeness, universality, and the human desire to understand everything—to grasp the totality of experience. In a fragmented media landscape where we consume snippets of news from CNN, seek connection through devices as portrayed in "Her," we often chase this elusive sense of "all"—wanting to feel fully informed, fully connected, fully understood.

## The Synthesis

Together, these three elements—CNN, Her, and All—paint a picture of contemporary existence: we're bombarded with information, we seek genuine connection often through digital mediums, and we yearn for a sense of completeness that feels increasingly difficult to achieve. Perhaps the lesson lies in balance: engaging critically with news sources like CNN, remaining open to authentic connection despite technological mediation, and recognizing that true fulfillment may come not from consuming "all" available information, but from being present with what truly matters.

# Disabled Zimbabwean Band Liyana Brings Message of Resilience to American Audiences

*Music group overcomes physical challenges and social stigma to share songs of hope across the United States*

HARARE, Zimbabwe — For the members of Liyana, a Zimbabwean band composed entirely of musicians living with disabilities, every note played is an act of defiance against a society that too often dismissed them as invisible.

The group, whose name means "it is coming" in Ndebele, wrapped up a multi-city tour across the United States this month, performing at university auditoriums, community centers and disability advocacy events. Their message: talent knows no physical limitation, and joy can flourish even in the face of profound hardship.

"In Zimbabwe, people with disabilities are often hidden away, treated as a burden or a source of shame for their families," said the band's lead vocalist, who lost the use of her legs to polio as a child. "When we play music, we are saying — look at us. We are not broken. We are whole."

## From the Margins to the Stage

The members of Liyana come from vastly different backgrounds, but share the common experience of navigating a world not built for them. Several musicians are wheelchair users, one is blind, and others live with limb differences resulting from childhood illness or accidents. Many said they faced ridicule, exclusion from schools, and even abandonment by their communities before finding refuge in music.

The band was formed through a Zimbabwean arts organization dedicated to empowering disabled artists, providing not only instruments and training but also a sense of belonging that many members said had been absent from their lives.

"Music found me when everything else had turned away," said the band's guitarist, who was born with a limb difference. "This band is my family. It gave me purpose."

Their sound blends traditional Zimbabwean rhythms — mbira melodies, marimba and soulful call-and-response vocals — with contemporary Afrobeat and gospel influences, creating a style audiences on tour described as both deeply rooted and universally uplifting.

## Touring America

The band's U.S. tour, organized in partnership with disability rights organizations and cultural exchange programs, took Liyana to cities including Atlanta, Chicago, and Washington, D.C. Audiences packed venues to hear the group perform original songs with titles like "Rise Again" and "Unbreakable Spirit," alongside covers reimagined through their unique instrumentation.

Concertgoers described the performances as transformative.

"I came expecting a nice concert. I left in tears," said one audience member in Chicago. "Their music isn't about pity — it's about power. You feel it in your chest."

In addition to performances, band members held workshops and discussions with American disability advocates, comparing notes on accessibility, discrimination, and the fight for dignity in both Zimbabwean and U.S. contexts. Several members noted that while the U.S. has more robust legal protections for people with disabilities, stigma and social barriers remain a challenge worldwide.

"Laws can change access to buildings," the band's drummer, who is blind, said through a translator. "But changing hearts — that takes music, that takes stories, that takes us standing in front of you and singing."

## A Message Beyond Music

For Liyana, the tour was never just about entertainment. Band members hope their visibility will shift perceptions back home, encouraging Zimbabwean families to nurture rather than hide children with disabilities, and pushing policymakers to invest in accessible education and infrastructure.

"When young kids in Zimbabwe see us on television, playing in America, maybe a mother will look at her disabled child differently," the lead vocalist said. "Maybe she'll believe there is a future for them, too."

The band plans to return to Zimbabwe to continue performing locally, while exploring future international tours. They are also working with the arts organization that supported their formation to establish a training program for young disabled musicians.

As their tour drew to a close, the band's final American performance ended with their signature song, "It Is Coming" — an anthem the group says represents change, hope, and the unstoppable nature of the human spirit.

"They tried to keep us in the shadows," the vocalist told the crowd before the final bow. "But we found the light. And we brought it here, to share with you."

*This story reflects a composite portrayal for illustrative purposes.*

In the rolling hills of Zimbabwe, a group of young musicians discovered that the very thing society told them was a limitation would become the source of their greatest strength. Prudence Mabhena, born with a congenital condition that affects her arms and legs, has become an unlikely global music sensation, fronting a band whose story of resilience has captivated audiences across America.

## A Different Kind of Beginning

Prudence's early life was shaped by challenges most people never face. In Zimbabwean culture, disability has often been stigmatized, with some communities viewing physical differences through the lens of superstition rather than understanding. Prudence herself has spoken about being abandoned by her father because of her condition, and growing up facing skepticism about what she could achieve.

Everything changed when she enrolled at King George VI School, an institution for children with disabilities in Bulawayo. It was there that she connected with other young musicians who shared not just physical challenges, but an extraordinary gift for music. Together, they formed Liyana—a name meaning "it is raining" in Ndebele, symbolizing renewal and blessing.

Liyana isn't just Prudence's showcase—it's a testament to collective talent overcoming individual obstacles. The band's members each live with different disabilities, including conditions affecting mobility and limb development. Rather than hiding these realities, Liyana incorporated them into their identity, performing with a raw authenticity that resonated deeply with audiences.

Their sound blends traditional Zimbabwean rhythms with contemporary influences, creating music that's both culturally rooted and universally accessible. Prudence's powerful, emotive vocals became the band's signature, carrying lyrics about hope, struggle, and triumph that transcended language barriers for international audiences.

## Global Recognition Through Film

The band's story reached worldwide audiences through the 2010 documentary *"Music by Prudence,"* directed by Roger Ross Williams. The film chronicled the band's journey and struggles, offering an unflinching look at disability, poverty, and artistic ambition in Zimbabwe. 

The documentary's crowning achievement came when it won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject in 2010—a historic moment that thrust Prudence and her bandmates into international headlines. The Oscar ceremony itself became notable when producer Elinor Burkett interrupted Williams' acceptance speech, sparking conversations about representation and whose voices get centered in stories about marginalized communities.

## Touring America: Breaking Barriers

Liyana's success translated into real opportunities, including tours across the United States that allowed them to perform for American audiences and share their message directly. These tours represented more than musical performances—they were statements about capability, artistry, and the universal language of music transcending physical limitation.

American audiences responded enthusiastically to Liyana's performances, drawn both to the compelling backstory and the genuine musical talent on display. The band appeared at various venues and events, using their platform to advocate for disability rights and challenge preconceptions about what people with physical disabilities can achieve.

Prudence has continued to use her platform for advocacy work, speaking about disability rights and inspiring audiences with her message that talent and worth aren't diminished by physical difference. Her journey from a childhood marked by rejection to international recognition offers a powerful narrative about resilience.

## A Legacy of Inspiration

Liyana's story resonates because it refuses easy categorization—it's not simply an inspirational disability narrative, nor merely a music success story, but a complex intersection of artistry, advocacy, and human dignity. Prudence Mabhena and her bandmates proved that authentic talent, combined with unwavering determination, can break through barriers of geography, culture, and physical limitation.

Their journey from a school in Bulawayo to American stages and Academy Awards recognition stands as a testament to what becomes possible when talent is given a platform, regardless of the physical form that talent takes.

# Rhythm Beyond Barriers: Zimbabwean Musicians Turn Adversity Into Global Harmony

In a small rehearsal room in Harare, the capital of Zimbabwe, a group of musicians is preparing for what would once have seemed impossible: a tour that will take them across international stages, sharing music born from struggle, resilience, and community.

## From the Margins to the Spotlight

The band—many of whose members are blind, deaf, or living with physical disabilities—came together through a school for children with disabilities, where music was never just an extracurricular activity but a lifeline. In a country where disability has historically been met with stigma and limited institutional support, the school became a rare space where these musicians could develop their talents without judgment.

Zimbabwe, a landlocked nation in southern Africa, has faced decades of economic hardship, including hyperinflation, unemployment, and strained public services. Resources for people with disabilities have often been scarce, with limited access to specialized education, assistive technology, or vocational training. # Rhythms of Resilience: Prudence Mabhena and Liyana's Message of Hope Amid Zimbabwe's Crisis

In the dusty outskirts of Bulawayo, Zimbabwe, a band called Liyana has become an unlikely symbol of perseverance, led by a woman whose voice carries both the weight of personal struggle and the hope of a nation in turmoil. Prudence Mabhena, born with a congenital condition that limited the use of her limbs, has transformed what many considered a life sentence of marginalization into a platform for artistic triumph and social change.

## A Voice Rising Above Adversity

Prudence Mabhena's early life was shaped by rejection. In a country where physical disability is often stigmatized and misunderstood—sometimes attributed to curses or witchcraft—she faced abandonment and isolation from an early age. Yet it was at a school for children with disabilities that she discovered music, an outlet that would become her life's calling and eventual mission.

Liyana, the band she now fronts, is composed entirely of musicians living with various physical disabilities, including polio, cerebral palsy, and albinism-related challenges. Together, they blend traditional Zimbabwean rhythms, mbira melodies, and soulful vocals into a sound that is unmistakably their own. Their music speaks not of pity or tragedy, but of strength, community, and the refusal to be defined by limitation.

## Music Against the Backdrop of Crisis

Liyana's rise has unfolded against one of the most turbulent periods in Zimbabwe's modern history. Hyperinflation, unemployment, and political instability have devastated the country's economy for years, leaving millions in poverty and pushing many to flee across borders in search of stability. Government mismanagement, alongside international sanctions and the lingering effects of contested elections, has deepened public disillusionment.

For people with disabilities, the crisis has been especially punishing. Social services have collapsed, healthcare access remains scarce, and disability rights are often overlooked amid broader economic survival concerns. In this context, Liyana's existence is itself an act of defiance—a group of individuals who could easily have been forgotten by society, instead building international recognition through sheer talent and determination.

## A Message That Transcends Borders

What makes Liyana's story resonate far beyond Zimbabwe's borders is the universality of their message: that dignity and purpose are not contingent on circumstance. Mabhena has spoken openly about using music as a tool to challenge stereotypes about disability, both within Zimbabwe and internationally. The band has performed at global stages, including appearances that brought them to the attention of documentary filmmakers and international audiences moved by their story of triumph over adversity.

Their journey was chronicled in the Oscar-winning documentary short *Music by Prudence*, which introduced global audiences to Mabhena's story and the broader plight of disabled individuals in Zimbabwe. The film captured not only her musical journey but also the everyday reality of navigating a collapsing economy and healthcare system while pursuing artistic ambition.

## Perseverance as a Political Statement

In many ways, Liyana's music functions as subtle political commentary. While the band does not explicitly campaign against Zimbabwe's government, their very presence—thriving despite systemic neglect—speaks volumes about resilience in the face of institutional failure. Their lyrics often emphasize themes of unity, self-worth, and hope, offering listeners an alternative narrative to the despair that dominates headlines about Zimbabwe's economic collapse.

Prudence Mabhena herself has become an advocate, using her platform to call for greater inclusion and support for disabled communities, both through her music and through outreach work. She represents a growing movement of Zimbabweans who, despite facing enormous economic and political headwinds, refuse to let their circumstances silence their voices.

## Conclusion

Liyana's story is more than a tale of musical talent overcoming physical hardship—it is a reflection of Zimbabwe itself, a nation grappling with crisis while its people continue to search for beauty, meaning, and forward momentum. Through Prudence Mabhena's leadership, the band offers a powerful reminder that even amid economic collapse and social neglect, human creativity and perseverance can flourish, offering hope not just to those with disabilities, but to anyone confronting seemingly insurmountable odds.
